{{Short description|English physicist (1928–2018)}}
{{Use dmy dates|date=July 2016}}
{{Use British English|date=July 2016}}
'''Raymond Neil Wilson''' (23 March 1928 – 16 March 2018)<ref>[http://trauer.donaukurier.de/traueranzeige/dr-raymond-neil-wilson/53180330 Dr. Raymond Neil Wilson: Traueranzeige.] Donaukurier, accessed 17/3/2018</ref> was an English [[physicist]] and telescope optics designer, best known for pioneering the use of [[active optics]] in large telescopes.<ref name="3790 Raywilson" />

== Biography ==

Wilson's first degree was in physics from the [[University of Birmingham]], followed by studying engineering at [[Imperial College London]].<ref name="KAVLI">Ray Wilson section of [http://www.kavlifoundation.org/2010-astrophysics-laureate-biographies 2010 Astrophysics Laureate Biographies] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20141204110105/http://www.kavlifoundation.org/2010-astrophysics-laureate-biographies |date=4 December 2014 }}, Kavli Foundation website, accessed 23/01/2011</ref> After completing national service in 1952, he resumed his work on optics.<ref name="KAVLI"/> He then worked at Imperial College and at the [[National Physical Laboratory (United Kingdom)|National Physical Laboratory]] in the UK.<ref name="KAVLI"/> From around 1961, he spent 11 years as Head of the Design Department for telescopes at [[Carl Zeiss AG]] in [[Oberkochen]], Germany.<ref name="EAS"/>

In 1972 he became Head of the Optics and Telescopes Group <ref name="EAS"/>
at the European Southern Observatory ([[ESO]]), where he worked for the next 21 years, first in [[Geneva]] and then in [[Garching]], Germany. 
His major contributions have been in telescope optics and technology. In particular, he developed the concept of [[active optics]], which is now the basic principle on which modern large telescopes are constructed. The concept of active optics was developed first in ESO's [[New Technology Telescope]] (first light 1988), and then in ESO's [[Very Large Telescope]] (VLT).<ref name="EAS"/> (first light 1998). 

Wilson retired in 1993, writing a two-volume monograph ''Reflecting Telescope Optics'', a leading work in the field. He also extended the design of large telescopes to the next-generation designs that use three, four, and five mirrors.<ref name="EAS"/>

Wilson's other interests included history, economics, cosmology and biology.<ref name="KAVLI"/>

== Awards and honors ==

The awards bestowed for his work include the [[Karl Schwarzschild Medal]] (1993) and a share of the [[Kavli Prize]] (2010),<ref name="ESO">ESO archive of [http://www.eso.org/sci/publications/messenger/archive/no.142-dec10/messenger-no142-41-41.pdf Raymond Wilson Honoured with Two Prestigious Prizes], The Messenger 142 – December 2010, page 41 (archived version accessed 23/01/2011)</ref> as well as the [[Tycho Brahe Prize]] (2010).<ref name="EAS">[http://eas.unige.ch/documents/eas_prize_2010_wilson.pdf Tycho Brahe Prize 2010 Awarded to Telescope Designer], press release from the [[European Astronomical Society]], 19 April 2010, accessed 23/01/2011</ref> He has also been made Chevalier of the French [[Légion d'honneur|Legion of Honour]] (2003)<ref>[http://articles.adsabs.harvard.edu/full/2003Msngr.112...56W High honour to Ray Wilson] [Order of the French Legion of Honour], Richard West, ''The Messenger'', No. 112, p. 56 (June 2003)</ref> and has received the [[Prix Lallemand]] (2005) from the [[French Academy of Sciences]].<ref>[http://www.academie-sciences.fr/prix/prix_2005.htm Lauréats des Prix de l'Académie de Sciences en 2005] {{webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20100822140238/http://www.academie-sciences.fr/prix/prix_2005.htm |date=22 August 2010 }}, French Academy of Sciences website (in French), accessed 23/01/2011</ref> He was a fellow of the [[Norwegian Academy of Science and Letters]].<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.dnva.no/c26849/artikkel/vis.html?tid=40118|title=Gruppe 2: Astronomi, fysikk og geofysikk|publisher=[[Norwegian Academy of Science and Letters]]|language=no|access-date=5 September 2025|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20141006072021/http://www.dnva.no/c26849/artikkel/vis.html?tid=40118|archive-date=6 October 2014}}</ref>

On his retirement in September 1993, the Themistian asteroid [[3790 Raywilson]] was named in his honor. The name was proposed by [[Lutz Schmadel]] and endorsed by the Heidelberg Observatory, where the asteroid had been discovered by [[Karl Reinmuth]] 56 years earlier.<ref name="3790 Raywilson" />
